lead: An ideal solution has no special attraction or repulsion between unlike molecules. Then each component's partial pressure in the vapour is just its liquid mole fraction times its own vapour pressure: y_i P = x_i P_i^sat. That is Raoult's law. Most real pairs — ethanol and water, acetone and chloroform — disobey it, so one correction per component is added, the activity coefficient γ_i. The modified form y_i P = x_i γ_i P_i^sat is the working equation behind distillation, absorption and flash-drum design in every chemical plant.
prereq: You need: 6.1 for the equal-fugacity criterion, 6.3 for the P-x-y diagram, and Unit 5 for the activity coefficient and the Margules, van Laar and Wilson models.

blocks.text: At equilibrium every component has the same fugacity in the vapour and in the liquid, f_i^V = f_i^L (see 6.1). Writing each side in terms of composition gives the general starting equation.
y_i φ_i^V P = x_i γ_i f_i^L,pure(T, P)
blocks.where: y_i is the vapour mole fraction, x_i the liquid mole fraction, P the total pressure in kPa, φ_i^V the vapour-phase fugacity coefficient, γ_i the liquid-phase activity coefficient, and f_i^L,pure the fugacity of pure liquid i at the mixture temperature and pressure.

blocks.text: Three assumptions reduce this to Raoult's law.

items: Ideal-gas vapour: φ_i^V = 1. Acceptable up to a few bar.
Standard state is pure liquid i at the same T and P, with the Poynting correction neglected, so f_i^L,pure ≈ P_i^sat, the vapour pressure of pure i at T.
Ideal solution: γ_i = 1, meaning unlike molecules attract each other exactly as strongly as like molecules.

blocks.where: y_i and x_i are mole fractions in vapour and liquid, P the total pressure, and P_i^sat the saturation (vapour) pressure of pure component i at the system temperature T, in kPa. Both Σy_i and Σx_i equal 1.

blocks.text: For a pure component, x_i = y_i = 1, and the same equation collapses to P = P_i^sat, the vapour-pressure curve. Get P_i^sat from an Antoine correlation, ln P_i^sat = A − B/(T + C). Use each correlation exactly as tabulated: the constants come with a stated temperature unit (K or °C) and pressure unit (kPa or mmHg). Plug T in that stated temperature unit, get P_i^sat in the stated pressure unit, then convert the result to kPa (1 mmHg = 0.13332 kPa) before adding terms (see Unit 4, Clausius-Clapeyron equation). Benzene–toluene near 1 atm is the classic pair that obeys the law closely, because the two molecules are similar in size and shape.

sections.h3: Modified Raoult's law and the bubble-pressure recipe

blocks.text: Drop only the third assumption. Keep the vapour ideal and keep the pure-liquid standard state. All liquid non-ideality now sits inside γ_i, and γ_i depends on the whole composition, not on x_i alone (Unit 5).

blocks.where: γ_i is the activity coefficient of component i in the liquid at the system T and composition x, dimensionless, and γ_i → 1 as x_i → 1. The other symbols are as before.

items: Fix the temperature T and the liquid composition x_i.
Get every P_i^sat from Antoine at that T.
Choose an activity model — Margules, van Laar or Wilson — and evaluate every γ_i at the given x.
Add the partial pressures: P = Σ x_i γ_i P_i^sat.
Divide each term by P: y_i = x_i γ_i P_i^sat / P. Check that Σ y_i = 1.

blocks.text: Bubble temperature: P and x are known, T is not, and both P_i^sat and γ_i move with T. Guess T, compute the sum, and repeat until it equals the given P. Dew point: y and P are known; T is not, and x is not. Guess T, get P_i^sat, start with γ_i = 1. Compute x_i = y_i P/(γ_i P_i^sat), normalise the x_i so they sum to 1, recompute γ_i at that x, then evaluate Σ y_i/(γ_i P_i^sat). Adjust T (or P, if it is the dew pressure you want) and repeat until the sum equals 1.

blocks.where: K_i is the K-value (vapour-liquid equilibrium ratio) of component i, dimensionless. It is the number a stage-by-stage column calculation uses.
α₁₂ is the relative volatility of component 1 with respect to component 2. α₁₂ above 1 means the vapour is richer in component 1; distillation gets easier as α moves away from 1.

sections.h3: Working backwards: γ from data and from an azeotrope

blocks.text: Measured P, x and y give activity coefficients directly, with no model: γ_i = y_i P/(x_i P_i^sat). Do this at every data point and you have the experimental γ(x) curve; fit a model through it.

An azeotrope is faster still. There x_i = y_i, the composition cancels, and each component gives P = γ_i P_i^sat, so γ₁P₁^sat = γ₂P₂^sat = P. One azeotrope point therefore fixes two activity coefficients. A one-parameter model such as Margules, ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², is then solved for A on the spot; a two-parameter model needs the Gibbs-Duhem equation (Unit 5) as the second relation.

A minimum-boiling azeotrope has P above the ideal value, so γ_i > 1: positive deviation, unlike molecules repel. A maximum-boiling azeotrope has P below the ideal value, so γ_i < 1: negative deviation, unlike molecules attract.

The azeotrope also marks the limit of ordinary distillation. At x_i = y_i the driving force vanishes and a plain column cannot cross that composition; pressure-swing or azeotropic distillation with an entrainer is needed.

figure.caption: The bubble-pressure route: temperature and liquid composition go in, saturation pressures and activity coefficients come out, and their sum gives P and then y. The numbers are the worked example.

spec.title: Bubble pressure with modified Raoult's law
spec.aria: A five-step flow: given temperature and liquid composition, get saturation pressures from Antoine, activity coefficients from the Margules model, add the partial pressures to find P equal to 51.51 kilopascals, then divide to get y one equal to 0.7177.

examples.question: At 343 K a binary liquid has x₁ = 0.40. The saturation pressures at 343 K are P₁^sat = 60.0 kPa and P₂^sat = 20.0 kPa. The liquid follows the one-parameter Margules model, ln γ₁ = A x₂² and ln γ₂ = A x₁², with A = 1.20. (a) Find the bubble pressure P and the vapour mole fraction y₁. (b) Compare with ideal Raoult's law.
steps: Partial pressures: x₁γ₁P₁^sat = 0.40 × 1.5403 × 60.0 = 36.97 kPa; x₂γ₂P₂^sat = 0.60 × 1.2116 × 20.0 = 14.54 kPa.
Vapour composition: y₁ = 36.97/51.51 = 0.7177 and y₂ = 14.54/51.51 = 0.2823; the sum is 1.0000, as it must be.
The real pressure is 15.5 kPa above the ideal value. Both γ values exceed 1, so this is a positive-deviation system: component 1 escapes more easily than an ideal solution would allow.
examples.answer: P = 51.51 kPa with y₁ = 0.7177, against 36.0 kPa and y₁ = 0.6667 from ideal Raoult's law.
examples.check:
import math
x1, x2 = 0.40, 0.60
P1s, P2s, A = 60.0, 20.0, 1.20
g1 = math.exp(A * x2**2)
g2 = math.exp(A * x1**2)
p1 = x1 * g1 * P1s
p2 = x2 * g2 * P2s
P = p1 + p2
y1 = p1 / P
Pid = x1 * P1s + x2 * P2s
y1id = x1 * P1s / Pid
print(round(g1, 4))
print(round(g2, 4))
print(round(P, 2))
print(round(y1, 4))
print(round(Pid, 1))
print(round(y1id, 4))

traps: Applying plain Raoult's law to a pair with a known azeotrope. Ideal Raoult's law cannot produce an azeotrope at all unless the two P_i^sat are equal, so it will badly misfit ethanol–water.
Evaluating γ_i at the wrong composition. In the one-parameter Margules model γ₁ uses x₂² and γ₂ uses x₁²; swapping the two squares is the commonest slip in the exam hall.

Check which T unit and P unit the Antoine constants were fitted for. If they are in °C and mmHg, put T in °C, get P_i^sat in mmHg, then convert to kPa. Converting T to K first, or pressure only, gives nonsense.
Reusing γ_i across temperatures. Both P_i^sat and γ_i change with T, so a bubble-temperature answer cannot borrow activity coefficients from a bubble-pressure answer at another temperature.
Reading a dew point as a bubble point. At a dew point the given composition is y; substituting it as x gives a liquid far richer in the heavy component and the wrong pressure.

quiz.q: State Raoult's law and name the three assumptions behind it.
quiz.a: y_i P = x_i P_i^sat. The assumptions are: ideal-gas vapour, φ_i^V = 1; standard state is pure liquid i at the system T and P with negligible Poynting correction, f_i^L,pure ≈ P_i^sat; and ideal solution, γ_i = 1.

quiz.q: Why does benzene–toluene follow Raoult's law closely while ethanol–water does not?
quiz.a: Benzene and toluene are similar in size and polarity, so unlike-pair interactions match like-pair interactions and γ_i stays near 1. Ethanol and water hydrogen-bond strongly and unequally, so γ_i departs far from 1 and the mixture shows a minimum-boiling azeotrope.

quiz.q: At 350 K, x₁ = 0.30, γ₁ = 1.80, P₁^sat = 80.0 kPa, γ₂ = 1.05, P₂^sat = 40.0 kPa. Find the bubble pressure and y₁.
A measured point gives y₁ = 0.60 at P = 101.3 kPa, with x₁ = 0.30 and P₁^sat = 120.0 kPa. Find γ₁.
At 320 K a binary mixture has an azeotrope at x₁ = 0.35 and P = 55.0 kPa, with P₁^sat = 110.0 kPa and P₂^sat = 70.0 kPa. Find γ₁ and γ₂ there and classify the deviation.
quiz.a: At an azeotrope x_i = y_i, so γ_i = P/P_i^sat: γ₁ = 55.0/110.0 = 0.500 and γ₂ = 55.0/70.0 = 0.786. Both are below 1, so the deviation is negative and the azeotrope is a maximum-boiling one.

quiz.q: Why does the bubble-pressure calculation need no iteration while the bubble-temperature calculation does?
quiz.a: At fixed T the saturation pressures and the activity coefficients are fixed numbers, so P is one direct sum. At fixed P the temperature is unknown, and both P_i^sat and γ_i depend on T, so T must be guessed, the sum evaluated, and the guess refined until the sum equals P.

quiz.q: Define the K-value and the relative volatility.
quiz.a: K_i = y_i/x_i = γ_iP_i^sat/P, dimensionless. Relative volatility α₁₂ = K₁/K₂ = γ₁P₁^sat/(γ₂P₂^sat).

beyond: Not for the exam. Plant simulators pick one activity model per pair, usually NRTL or UNIQUAC, and fit it to measured VLE or infinite-dilution data; where no data exist, group-contribution methods such as UNIFAC predict γ_i from molecular fragments. Every column stage inside those programs runs the bubble- and dew-point loops shown here. Current research pushes the same fugacity equality into electrolyte and ionic-liquid systems by adding a Debye–Hückel term to γ_i. Search 'NRTL binary parameters', 'UNIFAC group assignment' or 'azeotropic distillation entrainer selection' to go further.
